{{Short description|Theorem in analytic number theory}}
In mathematics, '''Vinogradov's mean value theorem''' is an estimate for the number of equal [[sums of powers]].
It is an important inequality in [[analytic number theory]], named for [[I. M. Vinogradov]].

More specifically, let <math>J_{s,k}(X)</math> count the number of solutions to the system of <math>k</math> simultaneous [[Diophantine equations]] in <math>2s</math> variables given by
:<math>x_1^j+x_2^j+\cdots+x_s^j=y_1^j+y_2^j+\cdots+y_s^j\quad (1\le j\le k)</math>
with
:<math>1\le x_i,y_i\le X, (1\le i\le s)</math>.
That is, it counts the number of equal sums of powers with equal numbers of terms (<math>s</math>) and equal exponents (<math>j</math>),
up to <math>k</math>th powers and up to powers of <math>X</math>. An alternative analytic expression for <math>J_{s,k}(X)</math> is
:<math>J_{s,k}(X)=\int_{[0,1)^k}|f_k(\mathbf\alpha;X)|^{2s}d\mathbf\alpha</math>
where
:<math>f_k(\mathbf\alpha;X)=\sum_{1\le x\le X}\exp(2\pi i(\alpha_1x+\cdots+\alpha_kx^k)).</math>
Vinogradov's mean-value theorem gives an [[upper bound]] on the value of <math>J_{s,k}(X)</math>.

A strong estimate for <math>J_{s,k}(X)</math> is an important part of the [[Hardy-Littlewood method]] for attacking [[Waring's problem]] and also for demonstrating a zero free region for the [[Riemann zeta-function]] in the [[critical strip]].<ref>{{cite book | first=Edward Charles | last=Titchmarsh | others=Edited and with a preface by D. R. Heath-Brown | title=The theory of the Riemann Zeta-function | edition=Second | year=1986 | mr=0882550 | publisher=The Clarendon Press, Oxford University Press | location=New York | isbn=978-0-19-853369-6 }}</ref> Various bounds have been produced for <math>J_{s,k}(X)</math>, valid for different relative ranges of <math>s</math> and <math>k</math>. The classical form of the theorem applies when <math>s</math> is very large in terms of <math>k</math>.

An analysis of the proofs of the Vinogradov mean-value conjecture can be found in the Bourbaki Séminaire talk by [[Lillian Pierce]].<ref>{{cite journal |first=Lilian B. |last=Pierce|authorlink=Lillian Pierce|title= The Vinogradov mean-value theorem [after Wooley, and Bourgain, Demeter and Guth] |year= 2017| volume=69| issue=1134 | pages=1–80 | arxiv=1707.00119 | journal=Séminaire Bourbaki}}</ref>

==Lower bounds==
By considering the <math>X^s</math> solutions where

:<math>x_i=y_i, (1\le i\le s)</math>

one can see that <math>J_{s,k}(X)\gg X^s</math>.

A more careful analysis (see Vaughan <ref>{{cite book | first=Robert C. | last=Vaughan | title=The Hardy-Littlewood method | year=1997 | volume=25 | edition=Second | series=Cambridge Tracts in Mathematics | location=Cambridge | publisher=Cambridge University Press | isbn=978-0-521-57347-4  | mr=1435742}}</ref> equation 7.4) provides the lower bound

:<math>J_{s,k}\gg X^s+X^{2s-\frac12k(k+1)}.</math>

==Proof of the Main conjecture==
The main conjecture of Vinogradov's mean value theorem was that the upper bound is close to this lower bound. More specifically that for any <math>\epsilon>0</math> we have
:<math>J_{s,k}(X)\ll X^{s+\epsilon}+X^{2s-\frac12k(k+1)+\epsilon}.</math>
This was proved by [[Jean Bourgain]], Ciprian Demeter, and [[Larry Guth]]<ref>{{cite journal |first1=Jean |last1=Bourgain | first2=Ciprian | last2 = Demeter | first3 = Larry | last3 = Guth |title= Proof of the main conjecture in Vinogradov's Mean Value Theorem for degrees higher than three   |year= 2016| volume=184| issue=2 | doi=10.4007/annals.2016.184.2.7  | pages=633–682 | arxiv=1512.01565 | journal=[[Ann. of Math.]]|hdl=1721.1/115568 |s2cid=43929329 }}</ref> and by a different method by [[Trevor Wooley]].<ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1112/plms.12204|doi-access=free|title=Nested efficient congruencing and relatives of Vinogradov's mean value theorem|year=2019|last1=Wooley|first1=Trevor D.|journal=Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society|volume=118|issue=4|pages=942–1016|arxiv=1708.01220}}</ref>

If
:<math>s\ge \frac12k(k+1)</math>
this is equivalent to the bound
:<math>J_{s,k}(X)\ll X^{2s-\frac12k(k+1)+\epsilon}.</math>
Similarly if <math> s\le \frac12k(k+1)</math> the conjectural form is equivalent to the bound
:<math>J_{s,k}(X)\ll X^{s+\epsilon}.</math>

Stronger forms of the theorem lead to an asymptotic expression for <math>J_{s,k}</math>, in particular for large <math>s</math> relative to <math>k</math> the expression
:<math>J_{s,k}\sim \mathcal C(s,k)X^{2s-\frac12k(k+1)},</math>
where <math>\mathcal C(s,k)</math> is a fixed positive number depending on at most <math>s</math> and <math>k</math>, holds, see Theorem 1.2 in.<ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.4007/annals.2012.175.3.12|doi-access=free|title=Vinogradov's mean value theorem via efficient congruencing|year=2012|last1=Wooley|first1=Trevor|journal=Annals of Mathematics|volume=175|issue=3|pages=1575–1627|arxiv=1101.0574}}</ref>

== History ==
Vinogradov's original theorem of 1935 <ref>I. M. Vinogradov, New estimates for Weyl sums, Dokl. Akad. Nauk SSSR 8 (1935), 195–198</ref> showed that for fixed  <math>s,k</math> with

:<math>s\ge k^2\log (k^2+k)+\frac14k^2+\frac54 k+1</math>

there exists a positive constant <math>D(s,k)</math> such that

:<math>J_{s,k}(X)\le D(s,k)(\log X)^{2s}X^{2s-\frac12k(k+1)+\frac12}.</math>

Although this was a ground-breaking result, it falls short of the full conjectured form. Instead it demonstrates the conjectured form when

<math>\epsilon>\frac12</math>.

Vinogradov's approach was improved upon by Karatsuba<ref>{{cite journal | first=Anatoly | last=Karatsuba | title=Mean value of the modulus of a trigonometric sum| journal=Izv. Akad. Nauk SSSR Ser. Mat. | volume=37 | year=1973 | issue=6 | pages=1203–1227 | doi=10.1070/IM1973v007n06ABEH002080 | bibcode=1973IzMat...7.1199K | mr=0337817 | language=ru}}</ref> and Stechkin<ref>{{cite journal | first=Sergeĭ Borisovich | last=Stečkin | title=Mean values of the modulus of a trigonometric sum | journal=Trudy Mat. Inst. Steklov | volume=134 | year=1975 | pages=283–309 | mr=0396431 | language=ru}}</ref> who showed that for <math>s\ge k</math> there exists a positive constant <math>D(s,k)</math> such that

:<math>J_{s,k}(X)\le D(s,k)X^{2s-\frac12k(k+1)+\eta_{s,k}},</math>

where

:<math>\eta_{s,k}=\frac12 k^2\left(1-\frac1k\right)^{\left[\frac sk\right]}\le k^2e^{-s/k^2}.</math>

Noting that for

:<math>s>k^2(2\log k-\log\epsilon)</math>

we have

:<math>\eta_{s,k}<\epsilon</math>,

this proves that the conjectural form holds for <math>s</math> of this size.

The method can be sharpened further to prove the asymptotic estimate

:<math>J_{s,k}\sim \mathcal C(s,k)X^{2s-\frac12k(k+1)},</math>

for large <math>s</math> in terms of <math>k</math>.

In 2012 Wooley<ref>{{cite journal | first=Trevor D. | last=Wooley | title=Vinogradov's mean value theorem via efficient congruencing | journal=[[Ann. of Math.]] | volume=175 | year=2012 | pages=1575–1627 | doi=10.4007/annals.2012.175.3.12  | mr=2912712 | issue=3| arxiv=1101.0574 | s2cid=13286053 }}</ref> improved the range of <math>s</math> for which the conjectural form holds. He proved that for

:<math>k\ge 2</math> and <math>s\ge k(k+1)</math>

and for any <math>\epsilon>0</math> we have

:<math>J_{s,k}(X)\ll X^{2s-\frac12k(k+1)+\epsilon}.</math>

Ford and Wooley<ref>{{cite journal | first1=Kevin |last1=Ford |first2=Trevor D. | last2=Wooley | title=On Vinogradov's mean value theorem: strong diagonal behaviour via efficient congruencing | doi=10.1007/s11511-014-0119-0 | journal=[[Acta Math.]] | year=2014 | volume=213 | issue=2 | pages=199–236 | mr=3286035| arxiv=1304.6917 |s2cid=11603320 }}</ref> have shown that the conjectural form is established for small <math>s</math> in terms of <math>k</math>. Specifically they show that for

:<math>k\ge 4</math>

and

:<math>1\le s\le \frac14(k+1)^2</math>

for any <math>\epsilon>0</math>

we have

:<math>J_{s,k}(X)\ll X^{s+\epsilon}.</math>
